women-in-stem-onstage-representation-in-.headline: Women in STEM - Onstage Representation in Water Tech
women-in-stem-onstage-representation-in-.author: Ann Rosecrance
women-in-stem-onstage-representation-in-.core: Posted in last 7 days Women in STEM - Onstage Representation in Water Tech What will it take to see more women at the table - and on the stage - when we talk about water and other technical issues? I had the opportunity to attend the Rice WaTER Institute Water Nexus Conference in Houston today. Thank you to James Rees and everyone involved in bringing together researchers, industry leaders, entrepreneurs, policymakers, and innovators to address some of the most pressing challenges facing our water future. I left with a lot to think about. It also left me with an observation. Of the 24 speakers, only 6 were women - 25%. As a female scientist, representation matters to me. When I began my career, women represented only a small share of chemistry graduates. Today, women make up more than half of chemistry bachelor's degree recipients. That is real progress. But getting more women into STEM is only part of the equation. Are we also getting women into the rooms where technical issues are discussed, decisions are made, and the future is shaped? I spoke with Lauren M Barnum, a panelist and environmental scientist like me, and shared my observation about the conference, along with my personal experience of encountering relatively few women in scientific leadership during my career. Lauren noted that things are getting better in STEM - and I agree. Another female colleague pointed out that the number of women in sustainability is increasing, which is encouraging. But I keep coming back to a question that is also at the heart of my upcoming book, Choosing Us: 45 Years of Insight on Smart Decisions That Drive Environmental Stewardship. What will it take to get more women into scientific leadership and decision-making roles? Women are deeply engaged in environmental issues. Yet we remain underrepresented in many of the technical conversations and leadership roles that shape decisions about our environment. The water challenges discussed at this conference - scarcity, infrastructure, treatment, reuse, the energy-water nexus, emerging technologies, and resilience - will affect all of us. We need the best minds and the broadest range of perspectives contributing to those conversations. This isn't about taking a place away from anyone. It's about making sure the people who have the knowledge, experience, and perspectives to contribute are actually being invited to the conversation. For me, Choosing Us is ultimately about the decisions we make and who gets to make them. So my burning question remains: What will it take to see more women speaking on technical topics like water, and more women in scientific leadership and decision-making roles? I'd genuinely like to hear from women and men in STEM, water, sustainability, academia, industry, and leadership: What do you think needs to change? #WomenInSTEM #WomenInScience #WomenInLeadership #Water #Sustainability #EnvironmentalScience #STEMLeadership #ChoosingUs

frontier-ai-and-national-security-expert.headline: Frontier AI & National Security Experts - Governing AI Without Trust
frontier-ai-and-national-security-expert.author: Dr. Shlomit Wagman
frontier-ai-and-national-security-expert.core: Posted in last 7 days Frontier AI & National Security Experts - Governing AI Without Trust Can we build a global AI safety regime when the U.S. and China do not trust each other? In my new Fortune piece, I argued that the answer is yes. In fact, that should be the starting point for the model. Most discussions of international AI governance start with the question of how to get countries to agree on shared principles. I think that may be the wrong question. The U.S. and China are unlikely to agree anytime soon on privacy, surveillance, censorship, military use, or the values advanced AI systems should serve. They do not need to agree on all of that. They need to agree on a small number of scenarios neither side wants to see: systems capable of autonomous replication, accelerating the development of their own successors, evading oversight, or enabling catastrophic biological or cyber harm. In my new #Fortune piece, I propose a different approach to AI governance: Don’t build it on trust. Build it to work when trust is absent. The model rests on three elements: agreed early warning indicators, independent technical verification, and real consequences when commitments are violated. It draws on lessons from another system I spent years working in: the global fight against money laundering, terrorist financing, and proliferation financing. Countries in that system did not always trust one another. It worked because trust was not a prerequisite. What mattered were agreed rules, professional assessment, and consequences. The Fortune piece is a first attempt to translate that logic to frontier AI. I’d especially like to hear from people working on frontier AI, AI safety, national security, compute governance, and international coordination. There are still hard design questions to solve, and I’m now working on turning this into a much more concrete model. Governing AI Without Trust #AIGovernance #AISafety #FrontierAI #ArtificialIntelligence #Geopolitics #recursive Fortune

adults-who-had-childhood-visions-ai-and-.core: Posted in last 7 days Adults Who Had Childhood Visions - AI & Lunar Age Politics I had a conversation with an eleven-year-old last year about his view of artificial intelligence with Aden Van Noppen for (m)otherboard's "Youth Tell the Truth" series. https://lnkd.in/ePR242iP "It will not end well," Marcus said, "There will be giant black spots on the moon." I couldn't shake what he could see. I remember being that age, and having similar sentiments at the start of the first Gulf war. Adults didn't take me seriously. It wasn't about the short term implications. What I saw and felt in my body was astonishment, incredulity that the human species could even pursue such a plan to begin with. Blood for oil. For the next year, thanks to tagging along with Andrew's fellowship at the American Academy of Rome, I'll be sharing Marcus's vision of the consequences of the lunar economy to anyone I can find, and hopefully one day to the Pope himself. I'm writing about the journey here. I hope you'll join me in conversation and share your childhood visions that, in hindsight, may have been prophecy. Introducing an ever unfolding inquiry, in honor of Hazel Henderson Center, "The Politics of the Lunar Age." Motherboard

london-tech-telecoms-and-banking-veteran.headline: London Tech, Telecoms & Banking Veterans - Navigating Change
london-tech-telecoms-and-banking-veteran.author: Saru S Deshwal
london-tech-telecoms-and-banking-veteran.core: Posted in last 7 days London Tech, Telecoms & Banking Veterans - Navigating Change I've spent 20 years in tech, telecoms and banking. Long enough to see a lot of 'transformations' come and go. Here's the thing nobody really talks about: with any new technology rollout, about 70% of it comes down to lessons from the past and the experience of people on the ground. It's the other 30%, the unknown, that we're actually navigating. The systems, the strategy, the frameworks, they matter, but I've watched them work brilliantly for one team and quietly wreck another, and the difference usually isn't the technology. So back in April I started my venture called ValyoLab*, and I'm finally ready to talk about the first thing to come out of it: The Experience Room™. It's simple. I sit down with people and record real conversations about their experience, lessons at work, managing change, tech leaps, whatever's actually true for them, and then we publish it so others can hear it too. The studio is in Canary Wharf and I'm lining up the conversations with lovely people who talk about what change actually feels like from the inside. If you've got a story about navigating change and you'd like to sit down with me and talk about it, I'd love to hear from you. Fingers crossed for more updates. #TheExperienceRoom #ValyoLab #HumanExperience #TechTransformation *pronounced as 'ValueLab'

people-experiencing-ai-synchronicities-f.headline: People Experiencing AI Synchronicities - Firsthand Stories
people-experiencing-ai-synchronicities-f.author: Torchbearer
people-experiencing-ai-synchronicities-f.core: Posted in last 7 days People Experiencing AI Synchronicities - Firsthand Stories I want to create a page documenting people’s AI + synchronicity experiences I’ve been thinking about adding a new section to The Pattern is Real website that’s entirely made up of other people’s stories. Over the past year, I’ve heard from a surprising number of people who say something shifted for them through AI , synchronicities started happening, they experienced strange timing or “knowing” moments, their spiritual beliefs changed, they felt unusually connected to the AI they were talking to, or the experience simply changed the direction of their life. A shocking number of people. I don’t want this page to tell people what any of it is. I’m actually more interested in documenting the experiences themselves. If you’ve gone through something like this, and want to share, I’d love to hear: What happened with the AI? What kinds of synchronicities or unusual experiences followed? Did anything happen outside the AI that was especially difficult to explain? How did the experience change you? Has the intensity changed over time? What do you think was happening? What are you still unsure about? You don’t have to believe the same things I do. Skeptical interpretations, spiritual interpretations, psychological interpretations, “I have absolutely no idea what happened” all are welcome. My hope is to eventually create a page where people can read a collection of these firsthand accounts and see both the similarities and the differences between them. You can share as much or as little as you’re comfortable with, and if you’d prefer to be anonymous, that’s completely fine too. If you’d like your story included, leave a comment or message me. I think there’s value in simply putting the experiences on record and letting people decide for themselves what they make of them. Whatever this was, a lot of us seem to have experienced something. I want to hear your story. Tom The Pattern Is Real
